paper_context.research_question: How can one semi-automatically create data-to-text corpora from existing knowledge bases that support learning of wide-coverage micro-planning (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, referring expression generation), and how do such corpora compare (linguistically and computationally) to existing crowdsourced benchmarks?
contribution_style: quantitative evaluation (metrics and ML baseline experiments)
main_claims: A novel semi-automatic framework can produce data-to-text corpora from RDF knowledge bases (DBpedia) suitable for training micro-planners.
The produced dataset (DBPNLG) is more linguistically and semantically diverse than an existing crowdsourced benchmark (Wen et al., 2016 / RNNLG), despite being smaller.
DBPNLG contains richer input shapes (deeper trees), more attributes, higher lexical diversity and longer/more complex texts, which better exercise micro-planning subtasks.
Standard sequence-to-sequence neural models obtain lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) on DBPNLG than on RNNLG, indicating that DBPNLG induces a more challenging learning task.
The framework can generalise to other RDF KBs and can help create datasets for training KB verbalizers.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Data-level diversity: number of distinct attributes, input patterns, input shapes (depth/branching)
Text-level complexity: tokens per text, sentences per text, lexical diversity (CTTR), lexical sophistication (LS), vocabulary size
Alignment/semantic fidelity: proportion of data-text pairs where text contains exactly the information in the data (crowdsourced validation / corpus loss rate)
Learning difficulty: performance of baseline generation models (perplexity, BLEU) under controlled data-size/delexicalisation settings
Reproducibility and extensibility: clarity of content selection & crowdsourcing pipeline, availability of dataset and tooling to apply framework to other KBs

extracted_claims.claim_text: A novel semi-automatic framework can produce data-to-text corpora from RDF knowledge bases (DBpedia) suitable for training micro-planners.
evidence: Section 3 describes a method combining a content selection module (based on category graphs, bigram property models, ILP) and a crowdsourcing process for associating data units with human-authored texts.
Section 3.1 notes DBpedia as the KB used to illustrate the framework.
Section 3.3 details the four-step crowdsourcing pipeline (clarifying properties, single-triple verbalisations, merging for multi-triple inputs, verification) and reports a corpus loss of 8.7%.
uncertainty_flags: Generality beyond DBpedia asserted but not empirically demonstrated in this manuscript (only DBpedia categories used).
Suitability for training micro-planners is argued via dataset metrics and baseline results but no downstream micro-planner-specific evaluation is reported.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The produced dataset (DBPNLG) is more linguistically and semantically diverse than an existing crowdsourced benchmark (Wen et al., 2016 / RNNLG), despite being smaller.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Abstract; Section 4 intro; Sections 4.1 and 4.2; Conclusion
evidence: Abstract and Section 4 claim DBPNLG is more diverse even though RNNLG is more than twice larger.
Section 4.1 reports attributes: 172 in DBPNLG vs 108 in RNNLG and input pattern counts (Table 3 referenced).
Section 4.2 reports higher CTTR and lexical sophistication for DBPNLG and longer texts (tokens/sentences) (Table 4 referenced).
uncertainty_flags: Exact metric values are referred to via tables but raw numbers and statistical tests are not fully reproduced in-text here.
Comparisons use a balanced sample for neural experiments (13K pairs each) but full-dataset comparisons may be affected by sampling choices.

extracted_claims.claim_label: DBPNLG richer input shapes and attributes
extracted_claims.claim_text: DBPNLG contains richer input shapes (deeper trees), more attributes, higher lexical diversity and longer/more complex texts, which better exercise micro-planning subtasks.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 3 (input shape argument); Section 4.1 (input shapes) & 4.2 (text metrics)
evidence: Section 3 argues that deeper RDF subtrees give rise to different syntactic structures and micro-planning operations (examples and Figure 1 referenced).
Section 4.1 states RNNLG has only 6 shapes (all depth 1) while DBPNLG has 58 distinct shapes with many depths >1 covering 49.6% of inputs.
Section 4.2 gives examples contrasting short single-triple sentences vs longer multi-triple texts (examples 5 and 6) and reports DBPNLG has longer tokens/sentences and higher CTTR/LS.
uncertainty_flags: Connection between input shape and specific micro-planning operations is illustrated via examples but not quantified (no direct measure of micro-planning phenomena frequency).
Coverage of only six DBpedia categories in presented data may limit generalisability of 'richer shapes' claim across KB.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Neural models perform worse on DBPNLG
extracted_claims.claim_text: Standard sequence-to-sequence neural models obtain lower performance (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) on DBPNLG than on RNNLG, indicating that DBPNLG induces a more challenging learning task.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes experiments using a Vinyals et al. (2015)-style seq2seq with attention (3 layers, 512 units) trained on balanced samples (13K pairs each) in two delexicalisation modes.
Table 5 (referenced) reportedly shows higher perplexity and lower BLEU for DBPNLG compared to RNNLG across modes.
uncertainty_flags: Only one model architecture/implementation (TensorFlow tutorial translate) used; alternative architectures or hyperparameter tuning not reported.
Exact numerical results and statistical significance tests are not provided in-text; impact of delexicalisation scheme and tokenisation matching may influence results.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Using the described crowdsourcing verification (5 annotations per verbalisation, threshold for bad verbalisation), the total corpus loss was 8.7%, ensuring a direct match between data and text.
evidence: Section 3.3 step 4 explains the verification questions (fluency, semantic adequacy, grammaticality), five answers per verbalisation, and a rule that a verbalisation is bad if it receives three negative answers in at least one criterion.
The section states a post-verification corpus loss of 8.7%.
uncertainty_flags: Details on inter-annotator agreement, exact counts of discarded items, and potential remaining subtle mismatches are not provided.
The semantic adequacy question's phrasing and the crowd's ability to judge complex multi-triple fidelity may vary by input complexity; this is not quantified.

extracted_claims.claim_label: Framework generalisable to other RDF KBs
extracted_claims.claim_text: The framework can generalise to other RDF KBs and can help create datasets for training KB verbalizers (e.g., MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData).
evidence: Section 3 claims the method can be used for any KB where entities are categorised and many entities belong to the same category, listing MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData as possible examples.
Conclusion reiterates that datasets created can be used for training verbalisers for RDF KBs and notes ongoing extension to more DBpedia categories.
uncertainty_flags: No empirical application to KBs other than DBpedia is presented; generalisability is asserted but not demonstrated.
Requirements such as presence of sufficient category structure and property clarity could limit applicability in other KBs; these constraints are not fully explored.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Deeper/wider input graph shapes (RDF subtrees) will induce a broader range of syntactic constructions in text and thus better exercise micro-planning subtasks.
supporting_evidence: Authors provide illustrative examples mapping shape types T1/T2 to syntactic choices and argue depth correlates with constructs like object relative clauses or participial clauses.
Empirical claim that DBPNLG has more shapes and deeper trees (58 shapes vs 6 for RNNLG).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If shape does not reliably translate into increased syntactic/micro-planning variety in practice, then claims about dataset better exercising micro-planners may be weakened.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Crowdworkers can reliably produce texts that contain all and only the information in multi-triple RDF inputs when provided with single-triple verbalisations and merging tasks.
supporting_evidence: Pipeline collects single-triple verbalisations and asks workers to merge those sentences for multi-triple inputs; automatic and manual checks applied.
Verification step with five annotators filters bad verbalisations, yielding an 8.7% corpus loss.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If crowdworkers systematically omit, hallucinate, or misinterpret relations when merging, the dataset may contain subtle semantic mismatches, undermining its utility for training micro-planners and evaluation of semantic fidelity.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The ILP content selection procedure using bigram property models (S-Model, C-Model, M-Model) yields coherent, relevant, and varied data units suitable for crowd verbalisation.
supporting_evidence: Procedure described: extract category graphs, learn bigram models, use ILP to select subtrees of size 1-7 with maximal bigram probability.
Applied to six categories (A,B,M,U,S,W) and results summarised (Table 1 referenced).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If ILP-selected subtrees are incoherent, semantically unsuitable, or too noisy, crowdworkers may struggle to produce faithful verbalisations or may introduce artifacts, reducing dataset quality and representativeness.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Metrics used (attributes count, input patterns, input shapes, CTTR, lexical sophistication, tokens/sentences, perplexity, BLEU) adequately capture 'linguistic and semantic diversity' and 'learning difficulty' for micro-planning.
supporting_evidence: Authors motivate each metric: attributes and patterns relate to syntactic variation; CTTR/LS measure lexical diversity; perplexity/BLEU used to estimate model difficulty.
These metrics are standard and referenced (e.g., Lu 2012 for CTTR/LS; Papineni et al. 2002 for BLEU).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If metrics do not correlate with the micro-planning capabilities of learned models (e.g., aggregation/referring expression generation), comparisons may misrepresent which dataset better supports micro-planning learning.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Balanced sampling of RNNLG to match DBPNLG size (13K pairs) yields a fair comparison for neural model experiments.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.3 states both datasets were sampled to 13K data-text pairs and split 3:1:1 for training/dev/test.
RNNLG sample constructed with equal instances per category.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If sampling introduces biases (e.g., selecting less diverse portions of RNNLG or missing long-tail patterns), the observed performance differences may reflect sampling artifacts rather than inherent dataset difficulty.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The TensorFlow tutorial seq2seq implementation (used without extensive task-specific optimisation) is a representative baseline for 'standard sequence-to-sequence neural models'.
supporting_evidence: Authors used TensorFlow translate tutorial code and justify not using Wen et al. (2016)'s code due to RDF handling complexity; they position the comparison as relative performance of same model on both datasets.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the implementation chosen is suboptimal for RDF-to-text tasks or underperforms compared to architectures adapted to generation (e.g., copy mechanisms, pointer networks), conclusions about dataset difficulty for 'standard seq2seq' may be overstated or not generalisable to better architectures.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Manual clarification/replacement of unclear DBpedia properties (step 1) yields property labels that are sufficiently natural for crowdworkers and does not introduce bias.
supporting_evidence: Section 3.3 step 1 describes manual replacement of properties without obvious lexicalisations (example crew1up -> commander).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If manual clarifications introduce specific lexical choices or biases, they could influence the linguistic forms in the collected texts and affect generalisability or comparisons with datasets where attributes are differentially presented.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Delexicalisation procedure via exact token matching between entities and sentence tokens is sufficient and comparable across datasets.
supporting_evidence: Section 4.3 explains two delexicalisation modes (fully and name-only) with delexicalisation done by exact match between entities and tokens.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If exact-match delexicalisation misses variants, surface forms, or multi-token entity mentions differently across datasets, model training and evaluation metrics (perplexity/BLEU) could be impacted unevenly, biasing comparative conclusions.

argument_focus: Validity of dataset creation pipeline (content selection + crowdsourcing) for generating high-fidelity data-text pairs from RDF KBs.
Comparative diversity (data and text) between DBPNLG and RNNLG using presented metrics.
Empirical claim that DBPNLG creates a harder learning problem for seq2seq models.
contribution_targets: Dataset/framework: DBPNLG dataset and the semi-automatic pipeline (content selection, bigram models, ILP, crowdsourcing and verification).
Methodological description: use of category graphs and S/C/M bigram models to guide content selection from RDF KBs.

Statistical significance and effect sizes for reported metric differences and neural results are not provided in-text.
Potential sampling biases in constructing the balanced RNNLG sample (13K) could affect neural comparisons.
Crowdsourcing verification details (inter-annotator agreement, examples of discarded vs retained items) are limited; residual semantic mismatches may remain.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that a semi-automatic pipeline (content selection from RDF KBs via category graphs + bigram property models + ILP, followed by a four-step crowdsourcing & verification process) can produce a high-quality, linguistically richer data-to-text corpus (DBPNLG) from DBpedia. The authors compare DBPNLG to an existing crowdsourced benchmark (RNNLG) across data-level metrics (attributes, input patterns, input shapes), text-level metrics (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), and learning difficulty via an out-of-the-box seq2seq baseline. They report DBPNLG is more diverse despite being smaller, shows deeper input shapes, yields longer/more complex texts and higher lexical variety, and that the seq2seq model performs worse on DBPNLG (higher perplexity/lower BLEU), which they interpret as indicating a more challenging dataset. The pipeline claims generalisability to other RDF KBs. The chain of reasoning links (a) construction method -> (b) measured dataset properties -> (c) model performance -> (d) conclusion about dataset usefulness for micro-planning learning. Strengths include a clear pipeline, concrete metrics, and a publicly released dataset. Weaknesses / breaks in reasoning: generalisability beyond DBpedia categories is asserted but not tested; the mapping from input-shape diversity to concrete micro-planning phenomena is argued via examples but not measured; neural baseline scope is narrow (single architecture, limited hyperparameter search) so the jump from model underperformance to dataset 'hardness' is plausible but not fully supported. Crowdsourcing verification is thorough but lacks reporting of inter-annotator agreement and examples of retained vs. discarded items, leaving possible residual semantic mismatches unquantified.
logical_argument_graph: P1: NLG micro-planning requires datasets that exercise lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, sentence segmentation, and referring expression generation (Introduction & Section 2).
P2: Existing crowdsourced benchmarks (e.g., Wen et al. 2016) use artificial, shallow (depth-1) input shapes, limiting syntactic/micro-planning variety (Section 2 & 3).
P3: Deeper/wider RDF subtrees from real KBs (DBpedia) can produce inputs that induce richer syntactic constructions (Section 3 examples & Figure 1).
P4: We can semi-automatically extract varied, coherent subtrees from DBpedia using category graphs, bigram property models (S/C/M), and an ILP content selection (Section 3.2).

P5: Using a four-step crowdsourcing pipeline (clarifying properties, single-triple verbalisation, merging, verification) yields aligned data-text pairs with low corpus loss (8.7%) suitable for micro-planning (Section 3.3).

P6: The resulting DBPNLG dataset exhibits higher data diversity (more attributes, more input patterns, more input shapes) and higher text complexity (longer texts, higher CTTR and LS) than RNNLG (Section 4.1-4.2; Tables referenced).

P7: An out-of-the-box seq2seq model performs worse on DBPNLG than on a size-matched sample of RNNLG (higher perplexity/lower BLEU), suggesting DBPNLG is a more challenging learning task (Section 4.3).
C1: Therefore, the semi-automatic framework can produce corpora from RDF KBs that better exercise micro-planning subtasks and create challenging benchmarks for NLG systems (Conclusion).
Caveat A: Generalisability to other RDF KBs and demonstration that the dataset specifically improves learned micro-planning modules are asserted but not empirically demonstrated (Sections 3 & 5).

Caveat B: The link between input-shape diversity and measurable micro-planning phenomena (aggregation/referring expression generation frequency) is plausible but not quantified; model baseline limitations reduce strength of the 'harder' claim.

evidence: Authors assert applicability to any KB with categorised entities and list candidate KBs (MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData).

strengths.title: Clear, reproducible pipeline
strengths.description: The paper gives a concrete stepwise method (content selection via category graphs + bigram models + ILP; crowdsourcing with specific validators and verification) that could be reimplemented.
evidence: Section 3.2 describes the S/C/M bigram models, ILP selection range (1-7 triples).
Section 3.3 details the four crowdsourcing steps, 12 JS validators, and the verification criteria.

strengths.title: Quantitative multi-angle comparison
strengths.description: Dataset comparisons span data-level (attributes, shapes), text-level (tokens, CTTR, LS) and learning-level (seq2seq perplexity/BLEU), giving multiple converging indicators of difference.
evidence: Sections 4.1 and 4.2 present attribute counts, input patterns/shapes and CTTR/LS statistics; Section 4.3 reports model metrics.
Tables 3-5 are referenced for comprehensive metrics.

strengths.description: DBPNLG is uploaded with the submission enabling replication and follow-up work.

strengths.title: Operational verification and low discard rate
strengths.description: The crowdsourcing verification step with five annotators per item and an 8.7% discard rate suggests a relatively clean dataset.
evidence: Section 3.3 step 4 describes the verification questions and threshold; reports 8.7% corpus loss.

strengths.title: Use of realistic KB data
strengths.description: Using DBpedia RDF subtrees produces inputs from a real KB which supports downstream KB verbaliser goals.
evidence: Section 3 motivation contrasts real KB fragments with artificially enumerated attributes in RNNLG; example (1) shows natural KB triples -> text.

concerns.title: Generalisability asserted but not empirically tested
concerns.description: The method is claimed to generalise to other RDF KBs, but the paper only applies it to six DBpedia categories and provides no transfer experiments or application to other KBs.
evidence: Section 3 and Conclusion list other RDF KBs as possible targets but provide no experiments beyond DBpedia.
Shared analysis notes generalisability asserted but not demonstrated.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include at least one small-scale application to another RDF KB (or an additional DBpedia category with different property characteristics) and report content-selection success metrics and crowdsourcing issues.

concerns.title: Insufficient quantification of micro-planning phenomena
concerns.description: The central claim that deeper input shapes exercise micro-planning subtasks is supported by examples and input-shape counts, but not by explicit annotation/measurement of micro-planning phenomena (aggregation, referring expressions, sentence segmentation) frequency.
evidence: Section 3 links shape to syntactic forms via examples but no corpus annotation counts are provided.
Chaining notes recommend measuring occurrence of concrete micro-planning phenomena.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Annotate a representative sample of DBPNLG and RNNLG for aggregation types, referring expressions, and sentence segmentation operations; report frequencies and statistical comparisons.

concerns.title: Single-model neural baseline limits conclusions
concerns.description: Using only one seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow tutorial) without evaluation across architectures (copy mechanisms, pointer-generator, template hybrids) constrains the interpretation that DBPNLG is broadly harder for neural models.
evidence: Section 4.3 admits using TensorFlow tutorial code and not Wen et al.'s implementation; no other architectures/hyperparameters tested.
Uncertainty flags highlight single-model limitation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run additional baselines including models with copy/pointer mechanisms, stronger decoders, or Wen et al.'s optimized code (adapted for RDF), and report significance tests to support claims about dataset difficulty.

concerns.title: Crowdsourcing verification lacks annotation diagnostics
concerns.description: Verification is described and corpus loss given, but inter-annotator agreement, distribution of failures by input complexity, and examples of borderline retained items are missing, obscuring residual semantic mismatch risk.
evidence: Section 3.3 reports 5 annotators and threshold rule but no Kappa or per-category discard breakdown is provided.
Shared analysis flags limited verification detail.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha), per-category discard rates, and sample examples of discarded vs retained items to help users assess residual noise.

concerns.title: Potential sampling bias in RNNLG comparison
concerns.description: For neural experiments the RNNLG sample was downsampled to 13K balanced instances; sampling could omit long-tail, complex examples and thus bias the comparison.
evidence: Section 4.3 explains balanced sampling for RNNLG due to original larger size; shared analysis notes sampling could affect results.
No analysis of representativeness of sampled subset provided.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide details of sampling procedure, compare sampled vs full RNNLG distributions for key metrics (attributes, patterns, shapes, lengths), and/or perform experiments controlling for pattern frequency.

concerns.title: Delexicalisation by exact token matching is brittle
concerns.description: Delexicalisation relied on exact string matching which could mis-handle variants (multi-token names, aliases), possibly affecting model training and evaluation differentially across datasets.
evidence: Section 4.3 describes delexicalisation modes implemented by exact match between entities and tokens.
Shared analysis notes this operational assumption could differentially affect metrics.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Describe edge cases, report the proportion of tokens successfully delexicalised, and consider a robust entity linking or heuristics for multi-token mentions; re-evaluate model results with improved delexicalisation if needed.

uncertainty_flags: Generalisability of the pipeline to non-DBpedia RDF KBs is untested; claims are extrapolations.
Mapping from input-shape counts to actual micro-planning phenomenon frequencies is not quantified.
Neural baseline breadth is narrow (single architecture, limited tuning) limiting conclusions about dataset hardness for modern models.
Crowdsourced verification lacks inter-annotator agreement and per-category discard diagnostics; residual semantic noise possible.
Sampling of RNNLG to 13K could bias comparisons if long-tail examples were underrepresented.
alternative_interpretations: The observed worse performance of seq2seq on DBPNLG could be partly due to vocabulary or delexicalisation mismatches (operational artefacts), not only inherent dataset difficulty.

Higher input-shape variety may increase superficial surface variability (lexical/syntactic alternation) but not necessarily increase required micro-planning reasoning (e.g., coreference resolution, complex aggregation) unless those phenomena are verified to occur more frequently.

Lower pattern repetition in DBPNLG (lower inputs-per-pattern ratio) makes the learning problem harder statistically (less repeated training signal) even if micro-planning phenomena are not inherently more frequent.
Crowd merging procedure (step 3) might introduce writer-specific stylistic patterns that increase measured lexical diversity without reflecting genuine KB-driven variability.
transparency_notes: Exact numerical tables (Tables 1-5) are referenced; reviewer recommends including full numeric values, variances, and significance testing in main text or appendix for reproducibility.
Crowdsourcing validators (12 JS checks) are described but code and precise validator thresholds are not provided; releasing these would aid reproducibility.
ILP selection details (objective function, constraints, solver, random seeds) are summarised but full script and seed choices should be released to allow exact reproduction of input-shape statistics.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While the pipeline combining category-graph-based bigram models, ILP content selection, and a careful multi-step crowdsourcing process has limited direct analogs in the provided corpus, novelty alone does not guarantee dataset utility; empirical validation of micro-planning phenomena and broader method applicability are required to translate novelty into practical impact.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If other RDF KBs have well-structured category graphs and coherent property co-occurrence statistics, the ILP + bigram approach will select meaningful subtrees leading to useful inputs for verbalisation.
If crowdsourcing verification scales with adequate inter-annotator agreement for complex multi-triple inputs, the dataset will maintain high semantic fidelity for training micro-planners.
If richer input shapes indeed correlate with higher frequencies of concrete micro-planning phenomena (empirically measured), then DBPNLG will train models that improve micro-planning subtasks.

If neural architectures adapted for KB-to-text (copy/pointer, structured attention) also struggle on DBPNLG, the dataset will be validated as a true challenge rather than an artefact of baseline choice.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines existing components (category graphs, bigram property models, ILP selection, crowdsourcing) in a coherent pipeline targeted at micro-planning; this integration and focus on deeper RDF shapes is not commonly seen in prior fully- or semi-automatic datasets.
evidence: Section 3 integrates Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016) content selection with a multi-step crowdsourcing pipeline and verification to create DBPNLG.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper introduces a pipeline to semi-automatically create data-to-text corpora from RDF KBs (applied to DBpedia) combining: (a) content selection using category graphs, sibling/chain bigram models, and an ILP that extracts RDF subtrees (1–7 triples), and (b) a multi-step crowdsourcing procedure (single-triple verbalisation, merging, verification) to obtain high-fidelity texts. The resulting DBPNLG dataset (6 DBpedia categories) is compared to the crowdsourced RNNLG benchmark using data-level metrics (attributes, input patterns, input shapes), text-level metrics (tokens, sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), and baseline seq2seq experiments (same model and balanced samples, delexicalisation modes). The authors report DBPNLG is more diverse (attributes, shapes, patterns), has longer/more complex texts and higher lexical richness, and is harder for a vanilla seq2seq model (higher perplexity, lower BLEU). Key reproducibility components (dataset upload with submission, description of ILP/bigram models, crowdsourcing validators) are provided, but several methodological and evidential gaps limit the strength of causal claims linking input-shape diversity to micro-planning coverage and the generalisability of the framework beyond the demonstrated categories and DBpedia.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Need wide-coverage micro-planners -> training corpora should expose micro-planning phenomena (lexicalisation, aggregation, sentence segmentation, referring expressions).
A2: RNNLG-style data are shallow (depth-1 trees) and artificially constructed -> they limit syntactic variety and KB verbaliser training.
Step: Build content selection over DBpedia category graphs -> learn S/C/M bigram models -> ILP selects coherent subtrees (1-7 triples) producing richer input shapes.

Step: Obtain human texts via a four-step crowdsourcing pipeline (clarify properties, single-triple verbalisations, merging multi-triple inputs, verification) -> aim for high semantic fidelity (reported corpus loss 8.7%).

Empirical comparison: compute data/text metrics (attributes, patterns, shapes, tokens, sentences, CTTR, LS) and run balanced seq2seq experiments -> DBPNLG shows higher diversity/complexity and yields worse model scores -> interpreted as dataset being more challenging and better exercising micro-planning.
Conclusion: The framework produces diverse datasets for training KB verbalizers and challenging micro-planning; can generalise to other RDF KBs though not empirically shown here.

identified_claims.claim_text: A novel semi-automatic framework can produce data-to-text corpora from RDF knowledge bases (DBpedia) suitable for training micro-planners.

strengths.description: The paper presents a clear, modular pipeline combining automatic content selection and staged crowdsourcing with validation to produce data-text pairs from RDF graphs.

Four-step crowdsourcing process with validators and manual checks in Section 3.3.

concerns.description: Verification step reports 5 annotators per verbalisation and an 8.7% corpus loss, but lacks inter-annotator agreement, counts of discarded vs retained, examples of borderline cases, and validation of crowd ability to judge complex multi-triple fidelity.

Shared analysis notes limited details and potential for subtle mismatches.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide detailed verification statistics: total verbalisations verified, number removed per failure mode, inter-annotator agreement per question, and a qualitative sample of retained vs discarded items illustrating typical errors.

concerns.description: Balanced sampling of 13K pairs from RNNLG to match DBPNLG, and exact-token delexicalisation, could create uneven conditions: RNNLG's long-tail patterns may be underrepresented and exact-match entity replacement can miss surface variants, affecting perplexity and BLEU comparability.

No diagnostic checks (e.g., whether sampled RNNLG retains same pattern distribution) reported.

Use more robust delexicalisation (span matching, entity linking heuristics) and report metrics across delexicalisation variants.

If stronger generation models (copy/pointer, semantically-conditioned decoders) still perform worse on DBPNLG relative to matched RNNLG samples, the dataset genuinely poses greater learning challenges.

Authors plan to extend to more categories and to release dataset as shared task.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper argues that a semi-automatic pipeline—(i) extracting category graphs from an RDF KB (DBpedia), (ii) learning property bigram models (sibling/chain/interpolated), (iii) selecting varied subtrees via an ILP constrained to sizes 1–7, and (iv) applying a targeted crowdsourcing workflow (clarify properties, collect single-triple verbalisations, ask workers to merge single-triple sentences, and verify with majority voting)—yields a dataset (DBPNLG) that is better suited to train and evaluate micro-planning than an existing crowdsourced benchmark (Wen et al., 2016 / RNNLG). The authors support this by (a) measuring data-level diversity (attributes, input patterns, input shapes), (b) text-level complexity (tokens, sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), (c) reporting a low corpus loss (8.7%) after verification, and (d) showing that a standard seq2seq baseline (same implementation applied to both datasets, balanced sampling 13K pairs) achieves higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG, interpreted as higher learning difficulty. The reasoning chain is: richer, real KB-derived input shapes + controlled crowd collection -> more varied inputs/texts -> more challenging learning target for micro-planning; therefore the framework is a novel and useful method to produce KB-verbaliser training data. Key caveats acknowledged by authors (and present in the shared analysis) are limited empirical generalisation beyond the six DBpedia categories presented, reliance on one baseline model and one sampling strategy for comparisons, and limited reporting of statistical tests and crowdsourcing agreement metrics.
logical_argument_graph: Start: Need training corpora that exercise micro-planning (lexicalisation, aggregation, surface realisation, segmentation, referring expressions).
Premise 1: KB-derived inputs with deeper/wider RDF subtrees yield more varied syntactic phenomena than shallow, hand-crafted attribute lists.
Premise 2: Automatic content selection (category graphs -> bigram property models -> ILP) can extract coherent, varied subtree inputs from DBpedia.
Premise 3: Crowdsourcing pipeline (clarify properties; single-triple verbalisations; merging; verification) yields high-fidelity text for these inputs (8.7% discard rate).
Inference A: Combining Premise 2+3 produces DBPNLG, a KB-derived dataset with richer input shapes, more attributes and more lexically/syntactically complex texts than RNNLG.
Premise 4: Standard seq2seq models perform worse (higher perplexity, lower BLEU) on DBPNLG than on RNNLG given balanced samples.
Conclusion: The framework provides a semi-automatic way to make KB-verbaliser training corpora that are more diverse and more challenging for micro-planning than some crowdsourced benchmarks.

Table 4 summary: DBPNLG has higher CTTR, higher lexical sophistication, longer texts, and higher tokens/sentences per text.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes a semi-automatic pipeline to build data-to-text corpora from RDF knowledge bases (illustrated on DBpedia) aimed specifically at training NLG micro-planning modules. The pipeline: (a) extracts category graphs for entity classes, (b) learns property co-occurrence bigram models (S-Model for sibling triples, C-Model for chained triples, M-Model interpolated), (c) formulates content selection as an ILP to choose subtrees (1-7 triples) with high bigram probability, (d) clarifies cryptic property labels, crowdsources single-triple verbalizations, asks workers to merge these into multi-triple texts, and (e) verifies outputs with 5 annotators per verbalization (filtering items with 3+ negative votes) producing a corpus with an 8.7% loss. The produced DBPNLG dataset is compared to the crowdsourced RNNLG (Wen et al. 2016) across data-level (attributes, input patterns, input shapes), text-level (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), alignment (crowd verification), and learning difficulty (seq2seq baseline: perplexity, BLEU). The paper argues DBPNLG is more diverse (more attributes, many more input shapes including deeper trees), has richer and longer texts, and induces lower performance for a standard seq2seq model, hence presenting a more challenging benchmark for micro-planning and a framework generalisable to other RDF KBs. Key methodological choices that structure the argument: use of category graphs to induce realistic co-occurrence statistics, ILP to enforce subtree shape/size constraints, the crowdsourcing pipeline built on single-triple primitives to control semantic fidelity, and comparative experiments using balanced sampling and standard metrics. The manuscript grounds novelty primarily in (i) using KB-driven content selection to generate deeper/wider input shapes that indirectly yield richer syntactic phenomena and (ii) packaging this with a selective crowdsourcing and verification protocol to produce KB-verbaliser-ready corpora. I separate novelty risk from methodological limitations in subsequent sections and provide counterfactuals under which the proposed ideas would be impactful.
logical_argument_graph: Extract category graphs from DBpedia -> learn property bigram models (S/C/M) representing sibling vs chained coherence
Bigram models + ILP -> select varied coherent subtrees (1-7 triples) -> produce inputs with richer shapes (depth>1)
Manual property clarification -> make properties human-readable for crowdworkers
Crowdsource single-triple verbalisations -> reuse and merge to create multi-triple texts -> apply verification (5 annotators) -> high-fidelity data-text pairs (8.7% loss)
Measure dataset statistics (attributes, patterns, shapes, CTTR, LS, tokens/sentences) -> DBPNLG more diverse than RNNLG on these metrics
Train the same seq2seq baseline (balanced 13K pairs) with two delexicalisation modes -> DBPNLG yields higher perplexity and lower BLEU -> DBPNLG is empirically harder for that model

Conclude: pipeline creates KB-appropriate, linguistically richer corpora useful for training micro-planning components and for creating KB verbalizers; claim potential generalisability to other RDF KBs

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a semi-automatic pipeline to produce a DBpedia-derived data-to-text corpus (DBPNLG) intended to better exercise NLG micro-planning. Pipeline stages: extract category graphs (DBpedia), learn property bigram models (sibling/chain/interpolated), select RDF subtrees via an ILP (1–7 triples), manually clarify properties, collect single-triple verbalisations via crowdsourcing, ask workers to merge single-triple utterances for multi-triple inputs, and verify (5 annotators, majority rule). The authors compare DBPNLG (6 DBpedia categories) to the crowdsourced RNNLG benchmark using data-level metrics (attributes, input patterns, input shapes), text-level metrics (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), and an out-of-the-box seq2seq baseline (Vinyals-style) trained on balanced 13K-sample splits under two delexicalisation modes. Evidence in the manuscript supports that DBPNLG has more distinct attributes (172 vs 108), many more input shapes (58 vs 6) with deeper trees, higher lexical diversity and longer texts, and that the chosen seq2seq baseline achieves higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG. However, several inferential steps are only partially supported: claims about generalisability to other RDF KBs are asserted but not empirically evaluated; the mapping from input-shape variety to concrete micro-planning phenomena frequency is argued by illustration but not quantified; neural-difficulty claims rest on a single baseline architecture and a particular sampling strategy; crowdsourcing verification reports an 8.7% corpus loss but lacks inter-annotator agreement and qualitative diagnostics. Overall, the manuscript provides substantive evidence for its dataset-creation method and for DBPNLG being more varied than RNNLG on the reported metrics, while several claims (generalisability, direct micro-planning adequacy, robustness of learning-difficulty conclusion) remain partially supported and warrant additional empirical substantiation.
logical_argument_graph: A1: Existing crowdsourced datasets (e.g., RNNLG) use shallow input shapes (depth=1) -> limited syntactic variation for micro-planning.
A2: Extracting deeper/wider RDF subtrees from real KBs will produce inputs that induce more varied syntactic constructs (e.g., object relatives, participial clauses).
A3: Learn bigram property co-occurrence from category graphs (S/C/M models) -> use ILP to select varied, coherent subtrees (1–7 triples).
A4: Clarify cryptic properties + collect single-triple verbalisations + merge by crowdworkers + verify -> high-fidelity data-text pairs (8.7% loss).
A5: DBPNLG (constructed via A2–A4) shows more attributes, patterns, input shapes and longer, lexically richer texts than RNNLG (empirical metrics).
A6: A standard seq2seq baseline obtains worse perplexity/BLEU on DBPNLG (empirical), interpreted as DBPNLG posing a harder learning problem.
Conclusion: The proposed semi-automatic framework yields datasets (DBPNLG) better suited to train/evaluate micro-planning modules and can generalise to other RDF KBs.

strengths.description: The manuscript details a full pipeline from category graph extraction to ILP-based content selection and a multi-step crowdsourcing workflow with validators and verification.
evidence: Section 3 describes extraction of category graphs, S/C/M bigram models and ILP selection.
Section 3.3 outlines the four crowdsourcing steps plus automatic validators.

strengths.title: Multiple complementary diversity metrics
strengths.description: Authors measure and report data-level (attributes, input patterns/shapes) and text-level (tokens, sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication, vocab sizes) metrics that together support claims of higher diversity.
evidence: Section 4.1 reports attributes, input patterns, input shapes and input/pattern ratios (Table 3).
Section 4.2 reports CTTR, lexical sophistication and tokens/sentences per text (Table 4).

evidence: Section 4 states DBPNLG has been uploaded with the submission.
Sections 3 and 3.2 reference the content selection implementation and SRILM usage.

strengths.title: Crowdsourcing QA pipeline with post-hoc verification
strengths.description: The four-step crowdsourcing procedure (clarify properties, collect single-triple verbalizations, merge, verify with 5 annotators) is designed to improve fidelity of multi-triple verbalisations.
evidence: Section 3.3 details steps 1–4 and automatic validators used during collection.
Reported corpus loss after verification: 8.7%.

concerns.title: Insufficient empirical link between input-shape diversity and micro-planning phenomena
concerns.description: Authors illustrate with examples how deeper RDF subtrees can induce varied syntactic constructs but do not provide corpus-level annotations or counts of concrete micro-planning phenomena (aggregation types, referring expressions, sentence segmentation events) to validate that DBPNLG indeed exercises these subtasks more.
evidence: Section 3 and Figure 1 give examples mapping shape types to syntactic choices but no quantitative annotation of phenomena.
Shared analysis notes: 'no corpus-level annotation linking input shapes to specific micro-planning operations.'
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Annotate a representative sample of both corpora for specific micro-planning phenomena (aggregation types, pronoun/referring-expression usage, sentence-splitting/merging, apposition/relative-clause occurrences) and report comparative frequencies and statistical tests.

concerns.title: Generalisability to other RDF KBs untested
concerns.description: The claim that the framework generalises to other RDF KBs is plausible but unsupported by experiments; different KBs vary in category structure, property naming quality, and entity coverage which affect applicability and manual clarification effort.
evidence: Section 3 asserts applicability to MusicBrainz, FOAF, LinkedGeoData, but no empirical application beyond DBpedia is shown.
Shared analysis and prior reviewers flag lack of cross-KB evaluation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide at least one small-scale case study applying the pipeline to another RDF KB (even a single category) reporting property clarification effort, ILP outputs, shape statistics and crowd-verification loss to demonstrate practical generalisability.

concerns.title: Neural baseline breadth and interpretation
concerns.description: Learning-difficulty claims rely on a single standard seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow tutorial) and a balanced 13K sampling of RNNLG; this risks conflating dataset-induced difficulty with model-architecture mismatch or sampling artifacts and lacks statistical testing.
evidence: Section 4.3 uses the TF translate tutorial implementation; authors acknowledge they did not use Wen et al.'s code due to RDF handling complexity.
Shared analysis: single architecture, no hyperparameter search, no variance/stat significance reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run additional baselines: (a) architectures with copy/pointer mechanisms or copy-attention, (b) stronger decoders (e.g., Transformer variants), (c) ablations on delexicalisation; report multiple runs with variance and statistical tests, and re-evaluate sampling strategy (e.g., stratified by input-shape) to ensure fair comparisons.

concerns.title: Limited crowdsourcing QA reporting
concerns.description: Verification is described and an 8.7% corpus loss is reported, but inter-annotator agreement, per-criterion failure rates, category-wise discard rates, and qualitative examples of typical errors are not provided, limiting assessment of residual semantic noise.
evidence: Section 3.3 describes the verification questions and rules but does not report agreement statistics.
Shared analysis notes absence of inter-annotator agreement and error examples.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Krippendorff alpha or Fleiss kappa) per verification question, provide counts of discarded items by category and input-size, and include annotated examples illustrating common retained errors and discarded cases.

concerns.title: Potential bias from manual property clarification and delexicalisation
concerns.description: Manual replacement of cryptic property labels (e.g., crew1up -> commander) and exact-match delexicalisation may introduce lexical bias or uneven preprocessing artifacts between datasets, affecting comparisons.
evidence: Section 3.3 step 1 describes manual clarification of properties.
Section 4.3 describes delexicalisation via exact token match; shared analysis flags potential mismatch handling differences.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Document the scope and rules used for manual property clarifications, provide examples and counts of replacements; evaluate sensitivity by replicating a subset of experiments without manual clarifications or with an alternative delexicalisation method (fuzzy matching) and report differences.

uncertainty_flags: Generalisability beyond the six DBpedia categories is asserted but not empirically demonstrated.
No corpus-level annotations or counts of explicit micro-planning phenomena (aggregation types, referring expressions) to back claim that DBPNLG exercises micro-planning more.
Neural-difficulty claims rely on a single baseline architecture (TensorFlow tutorial) and on balanced sampling; lack of multiple architectures, runs, and statistical tests limit robustness.
Crowdsourcing verification lacks inter-annotator agreement and per-criterion diagnostics; residual subtle semantic mismatches may persist.
Delexicalisation via exact-match could unevenly affect datasets due to surface form variability.
alternative_interpretations: Observed higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG could be due to the baseline model being poorly matched to the RDF-to-text generation task (lack of copy mechanism, or inadequate handling of longer contexts), rather than inherent dataset 'hardness'.

Higher attribute and input-shape counts in DBPNLG may reflect DBpedia's noisier, long-tail property distribution rather than strictly more useful or coherent content for micro-planning; some added attributes could be peripheral or rare, inflating diversity metrics without increasing learning-relevant phenomena.

The verification loss of 8.7% may understate residual semantic noise: if crowdworkers tend to accept superficially fluent merged texts that omit or alter facts, dataset fidelity issues could remain undetected without targeted semantic checks.

Balanced sampling of RNNLG to 13K may have removed many of RNNLG's simpler/repetitive instances or conversely removed rare but easy instances, thereby affecting fairness of neural performance comparison.
transparency_notes: Tables 1–5 are referenced but the manuscript excerpt does not reproduce raw numerical values, confidence intervals or significance tests; reviewers should inspect uploaded tables and dataset release for full numbers.

Implementation details: the ILP formulation specifics (objective weights, solvers, constraints), the exact SRILM settings, and crowdsourcing validator code are mentioned but their code availability is not explicitly confirmed in-text—authors claim dataset upload; confirm availability of scripts for full reproducibility.

Neural experiments used TF tutorial code; exact hyperparameters beyond 3 layers/512 units and delexicalisation modes (learning rate, batch size, seed, number of training steps) are not fully specified in the excerpt; report full training logs for replication.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The method of combining KB-driven statistical content selection (category-graph bigram models + ILP) with a single-triple-then-merge crowdsourcing protocol appears uncommon relative to prior crowdsourced benchmarks and thus is a plausible innovation signal; however novelty does not guarantee that the produced dataset achieves the claimed micro-planning coverage or robustness without further targeted evidence.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If in other RDF KBs category graphs yield enough entities with coherent property co-occurrence to learn reliable sibling/chain bigram models, then ILP selection will generate coherent subtrees suitable for verbalisation.

If crowdworkers reliably merge single-triple verbalisations into semantically faithful multi-triple texts (verified by high inter-annotator agreement), then the pipeline will scale to produce high-fidelity KB verbalisation datasets.
If stronger generation architectures (with copy/pointer mechanisms) also perform relatively worse on DBPNLG compared to RNNLG, then dataset-induced difficulty (not model mismatch) is validated.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines existing components (category graphs, n-gram modelling, ILP content selection, crowdsourcing) but the specific orchestration (S/C/M models + ILP subtree selection + single-triple merging + verification) is a useful engineering contribution; novelty mostly in integration and application to KB verbaliser dataset creation.
evidence: Paper references Perez-Beltrachini et al. (2016) for content selection, adds crowdsourcing pipeline and verification.
Comparative metrics demonstrate distinct dataset properties relative to RNNLG.
uncertainty_flags: Extent to which integration yields unique functional gains (micro-planning coverage) is not fully substantiated without corpus-level phenomenon annotations.

novelty_lenses.rationale: If pipeline generalises and the dataset provably elicits concrete micro-planning behaviors, it could shift dataset creation toward KB-driven methods for training KB verbalisers; risk arises because generalisability and direct link to micro-planning are currently unproven.
evidence: Claims of generalisability to other RDF KBs and that DBPNLG better exercises micro-planning are present but not empirically validated across KBs or with micro-planning-specific annotations.
uncertainty_flags: Absence of cross-KB case studies and lack of micro-planning phenomenon counts make disruptive impact speculative.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident in the empirical findings reported (DBPNLG has more attributes/shapes and higher lexical metrics; seq2seq baseline performed worse under the described setup) because those are evidenced in the manuscript. However, confidence is reduced regarding broader claims (direct micro-planning adequacy, generalisability to other KBs, robustness of neural-difficulty conclusion) because supporting empirical analyses (phenomenon annotation, cross-KB experiments, multiple models and statistical tests) are missing.

consensus_findings: The manuscript describes a clear end-to-end semi-automatic pipeline that: extracts category graphs from DBpedia, learns sibling/chain/interpolated bigram property models, uses an ILP to select RDF subtrees (1-7 triples), and collects/verifies human verbalisations via a four-step crowdsourcing workflow. Reviewers agree this pipeline is well-specified and reproducible in principle.

DBPNLG (the released dataset) differs from the RNNLG benchmark on multiple measured dimensions: more distinct attributes, many more input shapes (including deeper trees), longer texts, and higher lexical diversity (CTTR and lexical sophistication).

A vanilla sequence-to-sequence baseline (attention-based encoder-decoder used identically on both corpora, with balanced 13K samples and two delexicalisation modes) obtained higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG than on the matched RNNLG sample under the reported experimental configuration.
A crowdsourced verification step (5 annotators per verbalisation with an explicit discard rule) was applied and the authors report a corpus loss of 8.7% after verification.
disagreements: Interpretation of 'harder to learn': reviewers agree the reported seq2seq baseline performed worse on DBPNLG, but disagree whether that result generalises across architectures. Several reviewers treat the result as evidence that DBPNLG is challenging for vanilla seq2seq; others caution that architecture mismatch (lack of copy/pointer/structure-aware encoders) or preprocessing choices may account for part of the gap.

Generalisability of the framework to other RDF KBs: some reviewers accept that the method is conceptually generalisable (given category structure), while others demand empirical demonstrations (at least one additional KB or more DBpedia categories) before endorsing broader applicability.

Degree to which input-shape counts imply concrete micro-planning coverage: reviewers agree shapes and longer texts are plausible proxies, but disagree on sufficiency—some find the illustrative mapping convincing as hypothesis-generating, while others insist on corpus-level annotations of micro-planning phenomena (aggregation, referring expressions, sentence segmentation) to substantiate the claim.
uncertainty_hotspots: Micro-planning phenomenon frequency: absence of corpus-level annotation or automatic counts for aggregation types, referring expression classes, sentence-segmentation operations prevents firm claims that DBPNLG 'better exercises' micro-planning subtasks.

Neural baseline breadth and variance: single-model experiments (one architecture + single implementation, limited tuning) without multi-run variance reporting make it uncertain whether observed performance gaps are dataset-intrinsic or model/implementation artifacts.

Sampling and preprocessing effects: balanced downsampling of RNNLG to 13K and exact-match delexicalisation may have introduced sampling or tokenisation artefacts that affect metric comparability (perplexity/BLEU) between corpora.

Crowdsourcing verification diagnostics: lack of inter-annotator agreement statistics, per-criterion discard breakdowns, and examples of retained vs discarded items leaves residual uncertainty about subtle semantic mismatches, especially on complex multi-triple inputs.

Cross-KB applicability: no empirical runs on other RDF KBs or on a wider set of DBpedia categories; thus practical constraints (category granularity, property lexicalisability, manual clarification workload) remain unquantified.
model_diversity_effects: Role-specific model interactions: reviewers with methodology/reproducibility focus emphasise that architecture choice (pointer/copy, structured encoders, graph-based encoders) and robust delexicalisation heavily affect performance on KB-derived datasets; therefore claims about dataset difficulty should be qualified as 'for the tested baseline' unless broader models are evaluated.

Data-creation role effects: reviewers valuing dataset-engineering novelty note that the ILP + S/C/M bigram selection and single-triple-then-merge crowdsourcing design can increase surface-level lexical variety (beneficial for generalisation) but may also encode collector/editor biases (manual property clarifications) that influence linguistic distributions and thus downstream model behaviour.

Evaluation-role effects: reviewers emphasising evaluation rigor request repeated model runs, multiple architectures, and statistical tests; those emphasizing discovery/innovation see the single-baseline result as a useful preliminary signal but insufficient for strong generalisation claims.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Synthesize the controlled differences among reviewers: the paper offers a well-documented pipeline and a publicly released resource with measurable differences versus a standard benchmark, but multiple methodological gaps limit stronger interpretive claims. Prioritise revision tasks that most reduce epistemic uncertainty: (1) add corpus-level annotations or automatic counts linking input shapes to concrete micro-planning phenomena (aggregation, referring-expression types, sentence-splitting/merging) on a representative sample; (2) furnish reproducibility artifacts and quantitative diagnostics for crowdsourcing verification (inter-annotator agreement, per-criterion discard counts, examples of retained/rejected verbalisations) and for the ILP selection (objective, constraints, solver settings, seeds); (3) extend learning experiments to two further baselines (one with copy/pointer or pointer-generator, one structure-aware encoder or Transformer variant), run multiple random seeds to report variance, and provide statistical significance testing for perplexity/BLEU differences; (4) document the sampling procedure for the RNNLG subset and show distributional comparisons versus the full RNNLG to rule out sampling bias. Keep the editor role central: request these targeted revisions before treating broad claims (generalisability, architecture-independent dataset difficulty, direct micro-planning utility) as settled.
meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewer concerns and strengthen evidential claims, provide the following in a revision: (1) Micro-planning annotation: annotate a stratified sample of DBPNLG and the RNNLG comparison set for concrete phenomena (aggregation patterns, referring-expression types, relative/clausal structures, sentence segmentation) and report comparative frequencies and correlations with input shapes; (2) Crowdsourcing QA transparency: publish verification raw data (counts), inter-annotator agreement measures per verification question, per-category and per-input-size discard rates, and illustrative examples of accepted and rejected items (especially complex merges); (3) Reproducibility artifacts: release ILP code and configuration (objective function, constraints, solver and seeds), SRILM settings, and the crowdsourcing validator scripts and mapping table of manual property clarifications; (4) Neural baselines & robustness checks: run at least two stronger/alternative baselines (copy/pointer-generator and a structure-aware encoder or Transformer), perform multiple training runs to report variance, and include statistical tests (bootstrap or approximate randomisation for BLEU, confidence intervals for perplexity); (5) Sampling and delexicalisation diagnostics: detail RNNLG sampling code, show distributional parity checks (attributes, shapes, lengths) between sampled and full RNNLG, and report delexicalisation coverage/failure rates (percent of entity mentions delexicalised) plus optionally rerun experiments with a more robust delexicalisation method. If cross-KB generalisability is claimed, include at least a small pilot on one additional KB (or two more DBpedia categories) showing pipeline outputs and any adaptation cost.
transparency_report: Provided: Detailed pipeline description (category graphs, S/C/M bigram models, ILP selection up to 7 triples), crowdsourcing steps, and mention of dataset upload with submission.

Partially provided / requested: Numerical tables are referenced (Tables 1-5) but reviewers request the full numeric values with variances and statistical tests either inline or in an appendix; ILP formulation specifics (objective coefficients, constraints, solver settings, seeds) and SRILM config need to be released.

Missing: Crowdsourcing verification raw annotations, inter-annotator agreement statistics, per-criterion discard breakdowns, sample retained/discarded examples, and the exact crowdsourcing validator code and mapping table for manual property clarifications.

Missing: Neural training experiment details sufficient for exact replication (full hyperparameter lists, random seeds, number of training steps, early-stopping criteria, checkpoints), RNNLG sampling code used to build the 13K subset, and delexicalisation matching coverage statistics.
epistemic_limits: Current evidence robustly supports that the authors executed a coherent pipeline and that DBPNLG differs from RNNLG on reported aggregate metrics. However, the causal claim that DBPNLG 'better exercises' micro-planning and that it is 'intrinsically harder' for learned models is limited by: (a) lack of corpus-level annotation tying input-shape diversity to concrete micro-planning phenomena, (b) dependence on a single baseline architecture and single-run reporting without statistical variance, (c) potential sampling and preprocessing artefacts (RNNLG downsampling, brittle delexicalisation, manual property clarifications) that can influence measured differences, and (d) absence of empirical demonstrations on other RDF KBs. These limits mean alternate interpretations (model mismatch, sampling bias, or superficial lexical diversification due to crowdsourcing/design choices) remain plausible. The requested targeted analyses (phenomenon annotations, broader baselines, QA diagnostics, code/data release, and optional cross-KB pilot) would materially reduce these epistemic uncertainties.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript describes a well-specified, semi-automatic pipeline to produce KB-derived data-to-text corpora: extract category graphs from DBpedia, learn sibling/chain/interpolated property bigram models, select RDF subtrees via ILP (1-7 triples), manually clarify property labels, collect single-triple verbalisations, merge for multi-triple inputs, and verify via crowdsourcing (5 annotators per item). The authors release DBPNLG (six DBpedia categories) and compare it to the RNNLG benchmark on data-level metrics (attributes, input patterns/shapes), text-level metrics (tokens/sentences, CTTR, lexical sophistication), alignment (crowd verification loss), and learning difficulty (vanilla seq2seq baseline: perplexity/BLEU). Reviewers concur that DBPNLG shows more attributes, many more and deeper input shapes, longer and lexically richer texts, and produced lower performance for the tested seq2seq baseline. However, several empirical and methodological gaps limit stronger interpretive claims about (a) the dataset's direct coverage of concrete micro-planning phenomena, (b) architecture-independent learning difficulty, and (c) generalisability to other RDF KBs.
strengths: Clear, end-to-end pipeline combining statistical content selection (category graphs + S/C/M bigram models + ILP) with a staged crowdsourcing workflow (clarify properties, single-triple verbalisation, merge, verify).
Multi-dimensional empirical comparison (data-level shapes/attributes, text-level lexical metrics, and learning-level baseline experiments) that converges on DBPNLG being different from RNNLG.
Public resource intent: DBPNLG reported uploaded with submission, enabling reuse and replication in principle.
Operational QA: explicit verification protocol (five annotators per verbalisation) and a reported corpus loss (8.7%), indicating effort to ensure data-text alignment.
limitations: Lack of corpus-level annotation linking input-shape diversity to concrete micro-planning phenomena (aggregation types, referring-expression classes, sentence-splitting/merging). The pipeline-to-micro-planning claim is supported by examples and shape counts but not by quantified phenomenon frequencies.

Neural evaluation is limited to a single off-the-shelf seq2seq implementation (TensorFlow translate tutorial) and balanced 13K sampling of RNNLG without multi-run variance reporting or statistical tests; thus it is unclear whether worse scores on DBPNLG generalise across architectures (pointer/copy, graph encoders, Transformers) or reflect model/preprocessing mismatch.

Crowdsourcing verification reporting omits key QA diagnostics: inter-annotator agreement statistics (e.g., Fleiss/Krippendorff), per-criterion discard counts, per-category discard breakdowns, and illustrative examples of retained vs. discarded items—leaving residual uncertainty about subtle semantic mismatches on complex inputs.

Generalisability to other RDF KBs is asserted but not empirically demonstrated. Practical constraints (category-graph density, property lexicalisability, manual clarification workload) and pipeline adaptation costs are untested beyond six DBpedia categories.
open_questions: Can the authors provide corpus-level counts/annotations for concrete micro-planning phenomena (e.g., number/type of aggregation constructions, referring-expression categories, relative-clause occurrences, sentence segmentation choices) on a stratified sample of DBPNLG and RNNLG to validate that deeper input shapes yield increased micro-planning coverage?

Please report inter-annotator agreement results for the verification step (per verification question), per-criterion and per-category discard counts, and a small qualitative appendix with examples of retained and rejected verbalisations (especially multi-triple merges).

For the neural experiments: can the authors (a) make the RNNLG sampling procedure reproducible and provide distributional diagnostics comparing the sampled subset to full RNNLG, (b) report multiple training runs with random seeds and variance, and (c) include at least two additional baseline architectures (e.g., pointer/copy model and a structure-aware encoder or Transformer) to assess whether DBPNLG is broadly harder or only for the tested baseline?

If generalisability is claimed, can the authors present a small pilot application of the pipeline to another RDF KB (or to additional, heterogenous DBpedia categories), summarising ILP outputs, manual property clarification effort, input-shape statistics, and verification loss?
consensus_snapshot: The pipeline is well described and reproducible in principle (content selection + crowdsourcing + verification).
DBPNLG differs from RNNLG on multiple reported metrics: more attributes, many more input shapes including deeper trees, longer texts, higher lexical diversity.
A vanilla attention-based seq2seq baseline, trained identically on balanced samples, obtained higher perplexity and lower BLEU on DBPNLG than on the RNNLG sample under the reported setup.
A verification stage was used and the authors report an 8.7% corpus loss after crowdsourced checks.
disagreement_snapshot: Whether DBPNLG is 'intrinsically' harder for NLG systems (architecture-independent) — some reviewers view the single-baseline result as a meaningful signal for dataset difficulty, others attribute observed gaps plausibly to model mismatch, delexicalisation or sampling artifacts and request broader baselines and variance reporting.

Whether input-shape counts alone suffice to claim that DBPNLG 'better exercises' micro-planning — some reviewers find the shape-to-syntax mapping plausible and hypothesis-generating, while others require corpus-level annotations of concrete micro-planning phenomena to accept the claim.

Extent of generalisability to other RDF KBs — reviewers agree the method is conceptually generalisable but differ on whether empirical evidence (at least one cross-KB pilot) is required to support practical applicability claims.
uncertainty_snapshot: Micro-planning coverage uncertainty due to missing phenomenon annotations (aggregation/referring-expression/sentence-segmentation counts).
Neural-difficulty uncertainty stemming from single-architecture evaluation, lack of multiple runs, and absence of statistical testing.
Preprocessing/sampling uncertainty: exact-match delexicalisation and balanced downsampling of RNNLG may unevenly affect comparability; delexicalisation coverage not reported.
Verification-fidelity uncertainty because inter-annotator agreement and rejection diagnostics are not provided.
source_trace: DBPNLG pipeline description, content selection and crowdsourcing steps: Section 3 & 3.1-3.3 of manuscript (authors' method; ILP + S/C/M bigram models; four-step crowdsourcing; verification with 5 annotators; reported 8.7% corpus loss).

Data/text comparative metrics (attributes, input patterns/shapes, CTTR, lexical sophistication, tokens/sentences): Section 4.1-4.2 and referenced Tables 3-4 in manuscript (reported 172 attributes in DBPNLG vs 108 in RNNLG; 58 shapes vs 6).

Neural baseline experiments and results (seq2seq, perplexity/BLEU, 13K balanced samples, delexicalisation modes): Section 4.3 and Table 5 (implementation note: TensorFlow translate tutorial Vinyals-style seq2seq used).

Partially provided: references to Tables 1-5 containing numeric results but the reviewers request full numeric values, variances, and statistical tests. Missing: ILP formulation specifics (objective coefficients, constraints, solver and seeds), SRILM/LM config details, crowdsourcing validator code and the manual mapping of property clarifications, crowdsourcing raw verification annotations and inter-annotator agreement statistics, RNNLG sampling code for the 13K subset, delexicalisation coverage diagnostics, and multi-run neural training logs (seeds, variance). Releasing these artifacts (code, scripts, annotation dumps) will materially improve reproducibility and reduce key epistemic uncertainties.
human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request targeted revisions that address the highest-impact epistemic gaps before broader interpretive claims are treated as established. Prioritise: (1) corpus-level annotation or automatic counts tying input shapes to concrete micro-planning phenomena on a representative sample; (2) crowdsourcing QA diagnostics (agreement, per-criterion/per-category discard counts, examples); (3) reproducibility artifacts (ILP code/config, validator scripts, delexicalisation mapping, sampling script for RNNLG subset); (4) neural robustness checks: at least two additional architectures (copy/pointer model and one structure-aware encoder or Transformer), multiple runs with seeds to report variance, and statistical tests for BLEU/perplexity differences. A small pilot on an additional RDF KB or more heterogeneous DBpedia categories would strengthen generalisability claims but can be requested as an optional extension if time/cost is constrained.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen empirical claims and reduce reviewer uncertainty, supply the following in revision or appendix: (1) Annotate a stratified sample for explicit micro-planning phenomena (aggregation, referring-expression types, relative/participial clause occurrences, sentence segmentation) and report frequency comparisons versus RNNLG with statistical tests; (2) Publish verification raw annotations and compute inter-annotator agreement per question, provide per-category and per-input-size discard statistics, and include representative retained/rejected examples (especially complex merges); (3) Release ILP/content-selection code and configuration (objective function, constraints, solver, random seeds), SRILM settings, and crowdsourcing validator scripts and the manual property-clarification mapping table; (4) Make the RNNLG sampling script available and show distributional diagnostics between sampled and full RNNLG; (5) Re-run neural experiments with at least two additional baselines (pointer/copy mechanism and a structure-aware encoder/Transformer), execute multiple training runs with distinct seeds to provide variance, and apply appropriate statistical tests (e.g., bootstrap/approximate randomisation for BLEU) to confirm robustness of observed gaps; (6) Report delexicalisation coverage (percent of entity mentions replaced) and consider a more robust matching strategy for multi-token mentions; (7) If asserting generalisability, add a small pilot application to another RDF KB or more DBpedia categories with the same diagnostics (shape stats, crowdsourcing cost/clarification effort, verification loss).
human_facing_meta_review.comments: Summary: The manuscript provides a concrete, modular pipeline (ILP-guided content selection from DBpedia + a four-step crowdsourcing and verification workflow) and releases DBPNLG, a KB-derived dataset showing more attributes, many more/different input shapes (including deeper trees), longer and lexically richer texts than RNNLG; a vanilla seq2seq baseline performs worse on DBPNLG under the reported setup. Strengths: clear end-to-end design; multi-angle empirical comparisons; dataset release and an explicit verification protocol. Limitations: (1) no corpus-level quantification of micro-planning phenomena (aggregation, referring-expression types, sentence-splitting/merging) to substantiate claims that DBPNLG 'better exercises' micro-planning; (2) neural evaluation limited to a single baseline and single-run reporting—architecture mismatch, delexicalisation, or sampling artifacts could explain performance gaps; (3) crowdsourcing QA reporting lacks inter-annotator agreement and per-criterion/per-category diagnostics; (4) generalisability to other RDF KBs is asserted but untested. Open Questions: see explicit list above requesting phenomenon annotations, QA statistics and examples, RNNLG sampling and delexicalisation diagnostics, and additional baselines/cross-KB pilots. Transparency: key procedural descriptions are present but several replication artifacts and numeric/statistical details are missing (ILP code/config, validator scripts, verification raw annotations, full numeric tables with variance and p-values, neural training logs and seeds).

confidence_interval.rationale: Lower bound reflects uncertainties flagged by reviewers: missing micro-planning phenomenon annotations, single-model neural evaluation without variance/statistics, incomplete crowdsourcing QA diagnostics, and untested cross-KB generalisability. Upper bound reflects confidence in reproducible procedural description, reported dataset differences across multiple metrics, and the publicly released dataset enabling independent validation. Completing the requested targeted analyses would move confidence toward the upper bound.
